MULTISCALE MODELLING OF MATERIALS USING MACHINE LEARNING  ·  COURSE PROJECT
Effect of Porosity on an Additively Manufactured Aircraft Wing Bracket
From AlSi10Mg material data to bracket stress, with a physics-informed neural network and Ansys
TEAM
Pranav Parasuram C

slides.speaker_notes:
Good morning. We are presenting our course project on how porosity from 3D printing affects an aluminium aircraft wing bracket, and how a physics-informed neural network and Ansys work together to assess it.
1

slides.text:
01 · PROBLEM STATEMENT
Printed brackets are light, but they carry hidden pores
Problem
CAD & Ansys
EDA
Model
Evaluate
Deploy
1
The part: 
an aircraft wing-rib bracket that carries load from the rib into the wing spar.
2
The process: 
laser powder-bed fusion (metal 3D printing) in AlSi10Mg aluminium alloy, for low weight and complex shapes.
3
The catch: 
printing traps gas pores and leaves lack-of-fusion voids. Some porosity is always present.
4
The risk: 
each pore is a ready-made flaw. Under repeated flight loads it can grow into the crack that breaks the bracket.
Printed cross-section (schematic). Porosity φ = pore volume ÷ total volume.
Problem:  
how much does porosity reduce the size of flaw the bracket can safely carry, and how can a designer check that quickly?
2
slides.speaker_notes:
The bracket is printed, not machined, so it is light and can have an optimised shape. But printing always leaves pores. Each pore is a flaw already inside the part, and repeated flight loads can grow it into a crack. So our problem is: how much does porosity cut the flaw size the bracket can tolerate, and how can a designer check that quickly?
2

04 · CAD MODEL, LOADS AND SUPPORTS
Rib Bracket.STEP: geometry, loads and supports
Problem
CAD & Ansys
EDA
Model
Evaluate
Deploy
Envelope
231.5 × 230 × 40 mm plate
Volume · mass
778 cm³ · ≈ 2.1 kg (fully dense)
Material
AlSi10Mg, laser powder-bed fusion
Load F
Bearing load along +Y on the upper half of the Ø10 mm bore (628 mm² face)
Supports
Fixed in all directions on both 50 × 40 mm spar mounting faces
Reactions
R = F and M = F × 210 mm at the spar
Load path
Lower arm in tension, diagonal arm in compression
Why only the upper half? 
A pin can only push: it bears on the half of the bore the load drives it into, and the lower half opens a gap. Loading the whole bore would pull on the lower half and halve the bearing stress.
5
slides.speaker_notes:
This one slide carries the whole structural set-up. The bracket is a 40 mm thick AlSi10Mg plate with two arms meeting at a 10 mm bore. The pin load F acts upward on the upper half of the bore. Both mounting faces bolt to the spar and are fixed. Statics gives a reaction equal to F and a moment of F times the 210 mm lever arm, with the lower arm in tension and the diagonal arm in compression. We load only the upper half of the bore because a pin can only push; the lower half separates.
5

slides.speaker_notes:
We ran three explicit dynamics simulations in Ansys. They share the geometry, mesh set-up and bore load, and differ only in the material card. A is purely elastic. B is elasto-plastic, using Ansys' built-in Johnson-Cook strength model. C is our user-defined Johnson-Cook, where we type in the hardening curve point by point from our own customised Johnson-Cook law, which also carries shear modulus and porosity terms; in our fit the porosity exponent comes out at about zero, because density barely changes the stress in the data.

slides.text:
11 · CHOOSING THE NEURAL NETWORK
Why a physics-informed neural network (JC-PINN)
Problem
CAD & Ansys
EDA
Model
Evaluate
Deploy
Physics only
The JC equation alone is readable but too rigid: 10.24 error even on training cases.
Data only (plain MLP)
Fits familiar conditions well (2.17), but errs badly on unseen temperature–rate groups (11.90).
JC-PINN (chosen)
Chosen for its generalisation on unseen temperature–rate groups (6.24 vs 11.90 for the plain MLP) and its readable constants.
Selection used training cases only; the 37 held-out cases were not used. Group-holdout errors were part of the selection score, so they are mildly optimistic. 
In fairness: 
the same network with the JC equation switched off scored slightly better on those groups (5.63) and on test (0.338 vs 0.439), so the accuracy comes from the training recipe (strong weight decay, log-space output), not from the physics. All errors are curve RMSE; stress units inferred as MPa (unconfirmed).
12
slides.speaker_notes:
We compared approaches using only the training cases. The JC equation alone is readable but too rigid, about 10 units of error even on training cases. A plain MLP fits familiar conditions well, 2.17, but when a whole temperature-rate group is hidden its error jumps to 11.9. The JC-PINN multiplies the JC equation by a small learned correction; it scored 6.24 on hidden groups and keeps readable constants, which is why we chose it. Two honest caveats: those group errors were part of the selection score, so they are mildly optimistic; and the same network with the equation switched off did slightly better, 5.63 on groups and 0.338 against 0.439 on test. So the accuracy comes from the training recipe, strong weight decay and a log-space output, not from the physics itself. Units are inferred as megapascals.
12

All numbers are curve RMSE in stress units we infer to be megapascals. The plain MLP, 5-16-16-1 with 385 weights, scores 0.143 on the random 37-case test but 11.90 on the nine hidden temperature-rate groups. Our JC-PINN, the JC equation times a learned correction trained with 5 seeds, scores 0.439 on the test and 6.24 on hidden groups. slides.speaker_notes:
Before concluding, what we have not shown. First, evidence: the test set is not blind, case 60 is a single irregular case the model cannot fully reproduce, and nothing is validated against experiments. Second, definitions still to confirm: the stress units, what Svm and Evm mean, why every curve ends below where it starts, whether density and shear modulus stand for porosity, and which solver generated the data. Third, porosity: the fitted exponent is about zero, so the data show almost no porosity effect, and porosity is fixed at 4 percent as an assumption. Fourth, the critical flaw length is not computed yet: it needs the flaw geometry, a toughness source, the shape factor, the stress at the critical location and a rule for how porosity enters. We will confirm these with the professor.

CONCLUSION
What we showed, and what comes next
01
Realistic bracket model
Upper-half bore loading and fixed spar faces give a realistic load path; with plasticity the peak stress sits at the bore.
02
Plasticity matters
Elastic analysis overpredicts the peak by 1.85×; our user-defined JC matches Ansys' built-in JC within 0.94 %.
03
A material model with readable constants
JC-PINN predicts 37 held-out simulations to 0.44 mean RMSE (R² = 0.9995) and beats the plain MLP on unseen temperature–rate groups (6.24 vs 11.90, mildly optimistic).

slides.speaker_notes:
To conclude. Our bracket model loads the bore the way a pin does, and with plasticity the peak sits at the bore. Plasticity matters: an elastic analysis overpredicts the peak by 1.85 times, and our user-defined JC matches Ansys' own within one percent; those Ansys runs are the team's and were not re-run independently. The JC-PINN predicts the 37 held-out simulations to 0.44 mean error and beats the plain MLP on unseen groups, though that comparison is mildly optimistic. Next, and still planned: the porosity sweep, a toughness source, the flaw geometry and physical tests, then the bracket-check tool.
